tiers: None (untiered, all students sit the same papers; graded 9 to 1)

assessment.title: Explorations in Creative Reading and Writing
assessment.duration: 1 hour 45 minutes (includes a notional 15 minutes of reading time)
assessment.content: Section A: one 20th or 21st century prose fiction extract (reading, 40 marks, AO1, AO2, AO4). Section B: one descriptive or narrative writing task (40 marks, AO5, AO6).
assessment.format: Section A: Q1 short form (4), Q2 (8), Q3 (8), Q4 extended (20). Section B: Q5 one extended piece from a prompt or image (24 content and organisation, 16 technical accuracy).

assessment.title: Writers' Viewpoints and Perspectives
assessment.duration: 1 hour 45 minutes (includes a notional 15 minutes of reading time)
assessment.content: Section A: two linked non-fiction or literary non-fiction sources from different periods, one from the 19th century (reading, 40 marks, AO1, AO2, AO3). Section B: one viewpoint writing task (40 marks, AO5, AO6).
assessment.format: Section A: Q1 short form (4), Q2 (8), Q3 (12), Q4 extended (16). Section B: Q5 one extended piece giving a personal viewpoint for a stated audience, purpose and form (24 content and organisation, 16 technical accuracy).

assessment.title: Presenting, responding and Standard English
assessment.duration: Teacher-set; presentation guide of no more than about ten minutes
assessment.content: Assesses AO7, AO8 and AO9 through a formal presentation and responses to questions and feedback.
assessment.format: Teacher-marked on a competency basis; reported as Distinction, Merit, Pass or Not Classified. No marks. Does not count towards the 9 to 1 grade.

nonExam: Spoken Language endorsement (AO7 to AO9): a teacher-assessed formal presentation with questions, reported as a separate grade (Distinction, Merit, Pass or Not Classified), 0% of the GCSE grade.

aos.desc: Identify and interpret explicit and implicit information and ideas; select and synthesise evidence from different texts.
Explain how writers use language and structure to create effects and influence readers, using subject terminology.
Compare writers' ideas and perspectives, and how these are conveyed, across two or more texts.
Evaluate texts critically, supporting the view with appropriate textual references.
Communicate clearly, effectively and imaginatively; adapt tone, style and register; organise for coherence and cohesion.
Use a range of vocabulary and sentence structures for clarity, purpose and effect, with accurate spelling and punctuation.
Demonstrate presentation skills in a formal setting (Spoken Language).
Listen and respond appropriately to spoken language, including questions and feedback (Spoken Language).
Use spoken Standard English effectively in speeches and presentations (Spoken Language).

units.title: Subject content: reading across the course
points: Read fluently and critically a wide range of 19th, 20th and 21st century texts.
Texts include literature, literary non-fiction, reviews and journalism.
Evaluate and compare texts, and summarise and synthesise ideas across them.
Use reading to inform the student's own writing.
units.foundingYear: Not taught in 2027 (TGA opens in January): taught from Autumn 2027, as in the school's booklet.

units.title: Paper 1 Section A: Question 1, retrieval
points: Short-form question worth 4 marks, based on a stated range of lines in the extract.
Skill: identify and interpret explicit information and ideas (AO1).
Answers may quote or paraphrase; copying out a long section earns no credit.
Reading is of one 20th or 21st century prose fiction extract, printed on the paper.
units.foundingYear: Not taught in 2027 (TGA opens in January): taught from Autumn 2027, as in the school's booklet.

units.title: Paper 1 Section A: Question 2, language
points: 8 marks, on a short stated part of the extract.
Skill: explain how the writer uses language to create effects (AO2).
Bullet points on the paper are guidance only and carry no marks.
Subject terminology is credited, from simple to sophisticated use, but analysis of effect matters most.
The same skill is assessed again in Paper 2 Q3.
units.foundingYear: Not taught in 2027 (TGA opens in January): taught from Autumn 2027, as in the school's booklet.

units.title: Paper 1 Section A: Question 3, structure
points: 8 marks, on the structure of the whole extract.
Skill: analyse how the writer has organised the text for effect (AO2).
Advice: write in detail about two or three well-chosen structural features.
Sentence-level analysis counts only where it helps explain the structure of the whole text.
units.foundingYear: Not taught in 2027 (TGA opens in January): taught from Autumn 2027, as in the school's booklet.

units.title: Paper 1 Section A: Question 4, evaluation
points: Extended question worth 20 marks, the largest reading question on Paper 1.
Skill: evaluate the text critically, supported by textual references (AO4).
A statement is given and students decide how far they agree with it.
Marks reward the quality of evaluation, not which position is taken.
Responses may cover the writer's methods and the reader's response, with evidence.
units.foundingYear: Not taught in 2027 (TGA opens in January): taught from Autumn 2027, as in the school's booklet.

units.title: Paper 1 Section B: Question 5, descriptive or narrative writing
points: 40 marks: 24 for content and organisation (AO5), 16 for technical accuracy (AO6).
One extended task: describe or narrate, from a written prompt or an image.
The statement before the task sets the audience and purpose.
Marked on tone, style and register, plus organisation for coherence and cohesion.
Marked on vocabulary range, sentence variety, spelling and punctuation.
Notional 15 minutes of reading time is built into the 1 hour 45 minutes; leave time to check.
units.foundingYear: Not taught in 2027 (TGA opens in January): taught from Autumn 2027, as in the school's booklet.

units.title: Subject content: writing across the course
points: Write clearly and coherently in Standard English for different purposes and audiences.
Purposes named: describing, narrating, explaining, instructing, informing, arguing.
Use accurate grammar, punctuation and spelling, and a wide vocabulary.
Use rhetorical and creative techniques for impact.
units.foundingYear: Not taught in 2027 (TGA opens in January): taught from Autumn 2027, as in the school's booklet.

units.title: Paper 2 Section A: Question 1, true statements
points: 4 marks: choose the four true statements from a list that mixes true and false ones.
Skill: identify explicit and implicit information (AO1) in a stated part of Source A.
If more than four are chosen, only the first four in order are marked.
Two linked sources: one non-fiction and one literary non-fiction, from different periods including the 19th century.

units.title: Paper 2 Section A: Question 2, summary
points: 8 marks: a summary of the differences or similarities between the two sources, on a stated focus.
Skill: select relevant information and synthesise it across both texts (AO1).
Write in continuous prose, drawing inferences rather than listing quotations.
Use only material that answers the specific focus given in the question.

units.title: Paper 2 Section A: Question 3, language
points: 12 marks, on one source only (in the specimen, the 19th-century letter).
Skill: explain how the writer uses language to influence the reader (AO2).
Same skill as Paper 1 Q2, applied to non-fiction and literary non-fiction.
Subject terminology supports analysis of effect but does not replace it.

units.title: Paper 2 Section A: Question 4, comparison of perspectives
points: Extended question worth 16 marks, using the whole of both sources.
Skill: compare writers' ideas and perspectives and how they are conveyed (AO3).
Comparison should go beyond basic comprehension to methods: language and structure.
Both sources need balanced, supported coverage, with linking comparative language.

units.title: Paper 2 Section B: Question 5, viewpoint writing
points: 40 marks: 24 for content and organisation (AO5), 16 for technical accuracy (AO6).
One extended piece presenting the student's own view on a statement or theme linked to Section A.
Audience, purpose and form are stated (the specimen asks for a newspaper article).
Material from Section A may be used, but as the student's own view of it.
Rewards persuasive organisation, controlled register, varied sentences and accurate spelling and punctuation.

units.title: Spoken Language endorsement (AO7 to AO9)
points: A formal presentation of no more than about ten minutes, on a topic agreed with the teacher.
Students respond to questions and feedback from the audience (AO8).
Spoken Standard English must be used effectively and be audible and intelligible (AO9).
Graded Pass, Merit or Distinction on a competency basis; all criteria for a grade must be met.
Reported separately on the certificate; carries no marks and no weighting in the GCSE grade.

skills: Retrieving and interpreting explicit and implicit information with brief evidence.
Analysing word, phrase and sentence choices, and the effect on the reader.
Analysing structure across a whole text: shifts of focus, pace, sequencing.
Evaluating a text against a given statement with a supported, critical judgement.
Summarising and synthesising information from two sources in continuous prose.
Comparing ideas, attitudes and methods across texts from different periods.
Descriptive and narrative writing with deliberate crafting of language and structure.
Viewpoint writing in a stated form, for a stated audience and purpose.
Technical accuracy: sentence variety, punctuation, spelling, paragraphing.
Formal spoken presentation in Standard English, and responding to questions.

prerequisites.from: KS3 inference and retrieval from fiction (Years 7 to 9)
KS3 language analysis: word choice, imagery, effect (Year 8 War poetry, Year 9 Of Mice and Men)
KS3 narrative structure: openings, shifts, endings (Year 7 and Year 9 novels)
KS3 evaluation of writers' choices and reader response
KS3 descriptive and suspense writing, Year 5 and Year 6 sentence control
KS3 reading of non-fiction and persuasive texts; Year 8 war propaganda and persuasion
KS3 comparison of poems (Year 8 War poetry)
KS3 persuasive and formal writing; Year 6 formal writing
KS3 spoken English: presentations and debates

links.topic: 19th-century sources and viewpoints on events and reform
links.how: History supplies period context; English Language compares how writers convey attitude.

links.topic: Scientific controversies and public debate (e.g. vaccination, climate)
links.how: Science supplies accurate content; English Language summarises and compares how writers present evidence.

links.topic: Environmental issues and competing viewpoints on resources
links.how: Geography provides case-study evidence; English Language shapes it into a persuasive piece.

links.topic: Shared analysis of language and structure (AO2) and 19th-century writing
links.how: Literature applies analysis to set texts; Language applies it to unseen extracts.

links.topic: Images as prompts for descriptive writing
links.how: Art builds visual observation; English turns it into vivid description.

links.topic: Debating social issues and presenting a considered view
links.how: PSHE gives topics for discussion; English teaches formal delivery and responding to questions.

links.topic: Formal reports, letters and persuasive communication for an audience
links.how: Business models real audiences and forms; English teaches register and organisation.

links.topic: Online persuasion, bias and ethical debate about technology
links.how: Computing provides the topic; English analyses how language influences readers.

links.topic: Structured argument and presenting a reasoned viewpoint in formal speech
links.how: Islamic Studies gives discussion topics; English teaches argument structure and Standard English delivery.

Paper 1 mark splits (Q1 4, Q2 8, Q3 8, Q4 20, Q5 40) come from the specification; AQA mark schemes and levels descriptors were not read.
Paper 2 Q2 to Q4 focus wording is from the specimen paper and the AQA exam information note; live papers may vary the focus.
Spoken Language task options and the full Pass, Merit, Distinction criteria were summarised, not read line by line.
